title: OpenAI mistranslated mathematics into code for its Navier-Stokes proof
source_used: Yellow.com (same story as the New Scientist item); TechCrunch (C04-17) corroborates the paper
key_facts: A paper by Alexander Bastounis (King's College London) and Fabian Circelli and Anders Hansen (University of Cambridge) examined OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof announced on 8 Sep 2026.
They documented two places where the written argument and the Lean code diverge, including one where the code proves a weaker estimate than the paper states.
Lean is a programming language that lets a computer check a proof.
The authors say they make no claim about whether the written proof is correct; Lean confirms the final theorem but cannot show the intermediate steps are sound, so peer review is still needed.
OpenAI posted the 722 manuscripts on 6 Oct; summaries of the model's reasoning accompany only 10 results, and about 42% of the top-line results have been formalized in Lean.
The advisory group AGMAI issued guidelines on 29 Sep asking labs to stop testing advanced maths problems on proprietary models.
quote_evidence: They documented two places where the written argument and the Lean code diverge, including one where the code proves a weaker estimate than the paper states.
The authors said they make no claim about whether the written proof is correct.
why_it_matters_hint: Computer-checked proofs from AI may not match the argument humans read, so they still need human peer review.
event_date: Paper reported by 8 Oct 2026; OpenAI proof announced 8 Sep 2026
notes: New Scientist page returned 406; the same story was read at Yellow.com and TechCrunch. The "42%" figure appears in Yellow.com and is worded differently in TechCrunch, so it is not used in the entry. Follow-up of X30. Same cluster as C04-01, C04-06, C04-17.
